There is, sir, another self — divine, having material form, belonging to the sense sphere, feeding on solid food. That you do not know or see; that I know and see. Since, sir, that self is cut off and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, to that extent, sir, this self is completely cut off." Thus some declare the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
(c) Another says to him: "There is, sir, that self of which you speak; I do not say it does not exist. But this self, sir, is not to that extent completely cut off. There is, sir, another self — divine, having material form, made of mind, complete in all its limbs, not lacking in faculties. That you do not know or see; that I know and see. Since, sir, that self is cut off and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, to that extent, sir, this self is completely cut off." Thus some declare the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
(d) Another says to him: "There is, sir, that self of which you speak; I do not say it does not exist. But this self, sir, is not to that extent completely cut off. There is, sir, another self which, completely passing beyond perceptions of material form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, aware that 'space is infinite', has reached the field of infinite space. That you do not know or see; that I know and see. Since, sir, that self is cut off and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, to that extent, sir, this self is completely cut off." Thus some declare the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
(e) Another says to him: "There is, sir, that self of which you speak; I do not say it does not exist. But this self, sir, is not to that extent completely cut off. There is, sir, another self which, completely passing beyond the field of infinite space, aware that 'consciousness is infinite', has reached the field of infinite consciousness. That you do not know or see; that I know and see. Since, sir, that self is cut off and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, to that extent, sir, this self is completely cut off." Thus some declare the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
(f) Another says to him: "There is, sir, that self of which you speak; I do not say it does not exist. But this self, sir, is not to that extent completely cut off. There is, sir, another self which, completely passing beyond the field of infinite consciousness, aware that 'there is nothing', has reached the field of nothingness. That you do not know or see; that I know and see. Since, sir, that self is cut off and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, to that extent, sir, this self is completely cut off." Thus some declare the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being.
(g) Another says to him: "There is that self of which you speak; I do not say it does not exist. But this self, sir, is not to that extent completely cut off. There is, sir, another self which, completely passing beyond the field of nothingness, has reached the field of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. That you do not know or see; that I know and see. Since, sir, that self is cut off and destroyed with the breakup of the body and does not exist after death, to that extent, sir, this self is completely cut off." Thus some declare the cutting off, destruction, and non-existence of an existing being. These are the seven views.
The Sevens.
The Exposition of the Eights
(1) The eight grounds of defilement
Therein, what are the eight grounds of defilement? Greed, hate, delusion, conceit, views, doubt, dullness, restlessness — these are the eight grounds of defilement.
(2) The eight grounds of laziness

Therein, what are the eight grounds of laziness?
(a) Here a monk has work to do. He thinks: "I shall have work to do. But while doing the work my body will get tired. Well then, let me lie down." He lies down; he does not initiate energy for reaching the unreached, attaining the unattained, realising the unrealised. This is the first ground of laziness.
(b) Further, a monk has done work. He thinks: "I have done work. But while doing the work my body got tired. Well then, let me lie down." He lies down; he does not initiate energy for reaching the unreached, attaining the unattained, realising the unrealised. This is the second ground of laziness.
(c) Further, a monk has a journey to make. He thinks: "I shall have a journey to make. But while making the journey my body will get tired. Well then, let me lie down." He lies down; he does not initiate energy for reaching the unreached, attaining the unattained, realising the unrealised. This is the third ground of laziness.
(d) Further, a monk has made a journey. He thinks: "I have made a journey. But while making the journey my body got tired. Well then, let me lie down." He lies down; he does not initiate energy for reaching the unreached, attaining the unattained, realising the unrealised. This is the fourth ground of laziness.
(e) Further, a monk, walking for alms in a village or town, does not get his fill of coarse or fine food as much as he needs. He thinks: "Walking for alms in a village or town, I did not get my fill of coarse or fine food as much as I needed. My body is tired and unworkable. Well then, let me lie down." He lies down; he does not initiate energy for reaching the unreached, attaining the unattained, realising the unrealised. This is the fifth ground of laziness.
(f) Further, a monk, walking for alms in a village or town, gets his fill of coarse or fine food as much as he needs. He thinks: "Walking for alms in a village or town, I got my fill of coarse or fine food as much as I needed. My body is heavy and unworkable, like a load of soaked beans, I think. Well then, let me lie down." He lies down; he does not initiate energy for reaching the unreached, attaining the unattained, realising the unrealised. This is the sixth ground of laziness.
(g) Further, a slight illness has arisen in a monk. He thinks: "This slight illness has arisen in me. There is reason enough to lie down. Well then, let me lie down." He lies down; he does not initiate energy for reaching the unreached, attaining the unattained, realising the unrealised. This is the seventh ground of laziness.
(h) Further, a monk has recovered from illness, has recently recovered from sickness. He thinks: "I have recovered from illness, recently recovered from sickness. My body is weak and unworkable. Well then, let me lie down." He lies down; he does not initiate energy for reaching the unreached, attaining the unattained, realising the unrealised. This is the eighth ground of laziness. These are the eight grounds of laziness.
(3) The mind's resistance to the eight worldly conditions

Therein, what is the mind's resistance to the eight worldly conditions? Passion at gain, opposition at loss; passion at fame, opposition at disrepute; passion at praise, opposition at blame; passion at happiness, opposition at suffering — this is the mind's resistance to the eight worldly conditions.
(4) The eight ignoble ways of speech

Therein, what are the eight ignoble ways of speech? Saying one has seen what one has not seen, saying one has heard what one has not heard, saying one has sensed what one has not sensed, saying one has known what one has not known, saying one has not seen what one has seen, saying one has not heard what one has heard, saying one has not sensed what one has sensed, saying one has not known what one has known — these are the eight ignoble ways of speech.
(5) The eight wrongnesses

Therein, what are the eight wrongnesses? Wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration — these are the eight wrongnesses.
(6) The eight faults of a person

Therein, what are the eight faults of a person? (a) Here monks charge a monk with an offence. That monk, being charged with the offence by the monks, evades it through sheer forgetfulness: "I do not remember, I do not remember." This is the first fault of a person.
(b) Further, monks charge a monk with an offence. That monk, being charged with the offence by the monks, snaps back at the very one who charges him: "What is the use of the talk of a fool and incompetent like you! Do you really think you have something to say to me?" This is the second fault of a person.
(c) Further, monks charge a monk with an offence. That monk, being charged with the offence by the monks, throws the charge back at the very one who charges him: "You too have committed such-and-such an offence. You make amends first." This is the third fault of a person.
(d) Further, monks charge a monk with an offence. That monk, being charged with the offence by the monks, answers one thing with another, leads the talk aside, and displays anger, hate, and displeasure. This is the fourth fault of a person.
(e) Further, monks charge a monk with an offence. That monk, being charged with the offence by the monks, speaks waving his arms about in the midst of the Order. This is the fifth fault of a person.
(f) Further, monks charge a monk with an offence. That monk, being charged with the offence by the monks, disregarding the Order and disregarding the one who charges him, goes off wherever he likes while still bearing the offence. This is the sixth fault of a person.
(g) Further, monks charge a monk with an offence. That monk, being charged with the offence by the monks, saying "I have neither committed an offence nor not committed one", vexes the Order by remaining silent. This is the seventh fault of a person.
(h) Further, monks charge a monk with an offence. That monk, being charged with the offence by the monks, says: "Why are you venerable ones so extremely busy about me? Now I shall renounce the training and return to the lower life." Having renounced the training and returned to the lower life, he says: "Now, venerable ones, be satisfied." This is the eighth fault of a person. These are the eight faults of a person.
(7) The eight doctrines of the non-percipient

Therein, what are the eight doctrines of the non-percipient? "The self has material form and is unimpaired after death" — they declare it non-percipient; "the self is immaterial…"; "the self both has material form and is immaterial…"; "the self neither has material form nor is immaterial…"; "the self is finite and unimpaired after death" — they declare it non-percipient; "the self is infinite and unimpaired after death" — they declare it non-percipient; "the self is both finite and infinite and unimpaired after death" — they declare it non-percipient; "the self is neither finite nor infinite and unimpaired after death" — they declare it non-percipient. These are the eight doctrines of the non-percipient.
(8) The eight doctrines of the neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient

Therein, what are the eight doctrines of the neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient? "The self has material form and is unimpaired after death" — they declare it neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self is immaterial and unimpaired after death" — they declare it neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self both has material form and is immaterial and is unimpaired after death" — they declare it neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self neither has material form nor is immaterial and is unimpaired after death" — they declare it neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self is finite and unimpaired after death" — they declare it neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self is infinite and unimpaired after death" — they declare it neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self is both finite and infinite and unimpaired after death" — they declare it neither percipient nor non-percipient; "the self is neither finite nor infinite and unimpaired after death" — they declare it neither percipient nor non-percipient. These are the eight doctrines of the neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.
The Eights.
The Exposition of the Nines
(1) The nine grounds of resentment

Therein, what are the nine grounds of resentment? Resentment arises: "He has done me harm"; resentment arises: "He is doing me harm"; resentment arises: "He will do me harm"; "He has done harm… is doing harm… will do harm to one dear and pleasing to me" — resentment arises; "He has done good… is doing good… will do good to one disliked and displeasing to me" — resentment arises. These are the nine grounds of resentment.
(2) The nine stains of a person
Therein, what are the nine stains of a person? Anger, contempt, envy, stinginess, deceit, treachery, false speech, evil desire, wrong view — these are the nine stains of a person.
(3) The nine kinds of conceit

Therein, what are the nine kinds of conceit? The conceit of one who is better, "I am better"; the conceit of one who is better, "I am equal"; the conceit of one who is better, "I am worse"; the conceit of one who is equal, "I am better"; the conceit of one who is equal, "I am equal"; the conceit of one who is equal, "I am worse"; the conceit of one who is worse, "I am better"; the conceit of one who is worse, "I am equal"; the conceit of one who is worse, "I am worse" — these are the nine kinds of conceit.
(4) The nine things rooted in craving

Therein, what are the nine things rooted in craving? Because of craving there is seeking; because of seeking there is gain; because of gain there is deciding; because of deciding there is desire-and-lust; because of desire-and-lust there is holding fast; because of holding fast there is taking possession; because of taking possession there is stinginess; because of stinginess there is guarding; and with guarding as the occasion, there come to be the taking up of sticks and weapons, quarrels, contention, disputes, accusations, divisive speech, false speech, and many other evil, unwholesome things. These are the nine things rooted in craving.
(5) The nine agitations

Therein, what are the nine agitations? "I am" is an agitation; "I am this" is an agitation; "this I am" is an agitation; "I shall be" is an agitation; "I shall have material form" is an agitation; "I shall be immaterial" is an agitation; "I shall be percipient" is an agitation; "I shall be non-percipient" is an agitation; "I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient" is an agitation — these are the nine agitations.
(6-9) The nine imaginings and the rest

Therein, what are the nine imaginings… the nine waverings… the nine proliferations… the nine constructions? "I am" is a construction; "I am this" is a construction; "this I am" is a construction; "I shall be" is a construction; "I shall have material form" is a construction; "I shall be immaterial" is a construction; "I shall be percipient" is a construction; "I shall be non-percipient" is a construction; "I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient" is a construction — these are the nine constructions.
The Nines.
The Exposition of the Tens
(1) The ten grounds of defilement
Therein, what are the ten grounds of defilement? Greed, hate, delusion, conceit, views, doubt, dullness, restlessness, shamelessness, lack of moral dread — these are the ten grounds of defilement.
(2) The ten grounds of resentment

Therein, what are the ten grounds of resentment? Resentment arises: "He has done me harm"; resentment arises: "He is doing me harm"; resentment arises: "He will do me harm"; "He has done harm… is doing harm… will do harm to one dear and pleasing to me" — resentment arises; "He has done good… is doing good… will do good to one disliked and displeasing to me" — resentment arises; or resentment arises groundlessly — these are the ten grounds of resentment.
(3) The ten courses of unwholesome action

Therein, what are the ten courses of unwholesome action? Killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, wrong view — these are the ten courses of unwholesome action.
(4) The ten fetters

Therein, what are the ten fetters? The fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of wrong grasping of virtue and observances, the fetter of lust for existence, the fetter of envy, the fetter of stinginess, the fetter of ignorance — these are the ten fetters.
(5) The ten wrongnesses

Therein, what are the ten wrongnesses? Wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong knowledge, wrong liberation — these are the ten wrongnesses.
(6) The wrong view with ten grounds

Therein, what is the wrong view with ten grounds? "There is nothing given, there is nothing offered, there is nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit and result of well-done and badly-done actions; there is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father; there are no spontaneously reborn beings; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins of right conduct and right practice who declare this world and the other world, having realised them for themselves by direct knowledge" — this is the wrong view with ten grounds.
(7) The extremist view with ten grounds

Therein, what is the extremist view with ten grounds? "The world is eternal", or "the world is not eternal", or "the world is finite", or "the world is infinite", or "the soul and the body are the same", or "the soul is one thing and the body another", or "a Tathāgata exists after death", or "a Tathāgata does not exist after death", or "a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death", or "a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death" — this is the extremist view with ten grounds.
The Tens.
The Exposition of the Wanderings of Craving
(1) Concerning what is internal

Therein, what are the eighteen wanderings of craving concerning what is internal? There is "I am"; there is "I am thus"; there is "I am just so"; there is "I am otherwise"; there is "I shall be"; there is "I shall be thus"; there is "I shall be just so"; there is "I shall be otherwise"; there is "I am lasting"; there is "I am perishing"; there is "may I be"; there is "may I be thus"; there is "may I be just so"; there is "may I be otherwise"; there is "would that I might be"; there is "would that I might be thus"; there is "would that I might be just so"; there is "would that I might be otherwise".

And how is there "I am"? Not having discarded some thing — material form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness — one obtains the desire "I am", one obtains the conceit "I am", one obtains the view "I am". When that exists, there are these proliferations: "I am thus", or "I am just so", or "I am otherwise".
(2) And how is there "I am thus"? "I am a noble", or "I am a brahmin", or "I am a merchant", or "I am a worker", or "I am a householder", or "I am a renunciant", or "I am a god", or "I am a human being", or "I have material form", or "I am immaterial", or "I am percipient", or "I am non-percipient", or "I am neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "I am thus".
(3) And how is there "I am just so"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, so I am a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, so I am a brahmin", or "as he is a merchant, so I am a merchant", or "as he is a worker, so I am a worker", or "as he is a householder, so I am a householder", or "as he is a renunciant, so I am a renunciant", or "as he is a god, so I am a god", or "as he is a human being, so I am a human being", or "as he has material form, so I have material form", or "as he is immaterial, so I am immaterial", or "as he is percipient, so I am percipient", or "as he is non-percipient, so I am non-percipient", or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, so I am neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "I am just so".
(4) And how is there "I am otherwise"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, I am not so a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, I am not so a brahmin", or "as he is a merchant, I am not so a merchant", or "as he is a worker, I am not so a worker", or "as he is a householder, I am not so a householder", or "as he is a renunciant, I am not so a renunciant", or "as he is a god, I am not so a god", or "as he is a human being, I am not so a human being", or "as he has material form, I do not so have material form", or "as he is immaterial, I am not so immaterial", or "as he is percipient, I am not so percipient", or "as he is non-percipient, I am not so non-percipient", or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, I am not so neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "I am otherwise".
(5) And how is there "I shall be"? Not having discarded some thing — material form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness — one obtains the desire "I shall be", one obtains the conceit "I shall be", one obtains the view "I shall be". When that exists, there are these proliferations: "I shall be thus", or "I shall be just so", or "I shall be otherwise".
(6) And how is there "I shall be thus"? "I shall be a noble", or "I shall be a brahmin", or "I shall be a merchant", or "I shall be a worker", or "I shall be a householder", or "I shall be a renunciant", or "I shall be a god", or "I shall be a human being", or "I shall have material form", or "I shall be immaterial", or "I shall be percipient", or "I shall be non-percipient", or "I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "I shall be thus".
(7) And how is there "I shall be just so"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, so I shall be a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, so I shall be a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, so I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "I shall be just so".
(8) And how is there "I shall be otherwise"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, I shall not so be a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, I shall not so be a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, I shall not so be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "I shall be otherwise".
(9) And how is there "I am lasting"? Not having discarded some thing — material form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness — one thinks, "I am permanent, I am stable, I am eternal, I am not subject to change" — thus there is "I am lasting".
(10) And how is there "I am perishing"? Not having discarded some thing — material form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness — one thinks, "I shall be cut off, I shall be destroyed, I shall not be" — thus there is "I am perishing".
(11) And how is there "may I be"? Not having discarded some thing — material form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness — one obtains the desire "may I be", one obtains the conceit "may I be", one obtains the view "may I be". When that exists, there are these proliferations: "may I be thus", or "may I be just so", or "may I be otherwise".
(12) And how is there "may I be thus"? "May I be a noble", or "may I be a brahmin", or "may I be a merchant", or "may I be a worker", or "may I be a householder", or "may I be a renunciant", or "may I be a god", or "may I be a human being", or "may I have material form", or "may I be immaterial", or "may I be percipient", or "may I be non-percipient", or "may I be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "may I be thus".
(13) And how is there "may I be just so"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, so may I be a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, so may I be a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, so may I be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "may I be just so".
(14) And how is there "may I be otherwise"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, may I not so be a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, may I not so be a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, may I not so be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "may I be otherwise".
(15) And how is there "would that I might be"? Not having discarded some thing — material form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness — one obtains the desire "would that I might be", one obtains the conceit "would that I might be", one obtains the view "would that I might be". When that exists, there are these proliferations: "would that I might be thus", or "would that I might be just so", or "would that I might be otherwise".
(16) And how is there "would that I might be thus"? "Would that I might be a noble", or "would that I might be a brahmin", or "would that I might be a merchant", or "would that I might be a worker", or "would that I might be a householder", or "would that I might be a renunciant", or "would that I might be a god", or "would that I might be a human being", or "would that I might have material form", or "would that I might be immaterial", or "would that I might be percipient", or "would that I might be non-percipient", or "would that I might be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "would that I might be thus". (17) And how is there "would that I might be just so"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, so would that I might be a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, so would that I might be a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, so would that I might be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "would that I might be just so".
(18) And how is there "would that I might be otherwise"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, would that I might not so be a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, would that I might not so be a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, would that I might not so be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "would that I might be otherwise".
These are the eighteen wanderings of craving concerning what is internal.
(2) Concerning what is external

Therein, what are the eighteen wanderings of craving concerning what is external? There is "by this I am"; there is "by this I am thus"; there is "by this I am just so"; there is "by this I am otherwise"; there is "by this I shall be"; there is "by this I shall be thus"; there is "by this I shall be just so"; there is "by this I shall be otherwise"; there is "by this I am lasting"; there is "by this I am perishing"; there is "by this may I be"; there is "by this may I be thus"; there is "by this may I be just so"; there is "by this may I be otherwise"; there is "by this would that I might be"; there is "by this would that I might be thus"; there is "by this would that I might be just so"; there is "by this would that I might be otherwise".

(1) And how is there "by this I am"? Having taken up some thing — material form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness — one obtains the desire "by this I am", one obtains the conceit "by this I am", one obtains the view "by this I am". When that exists, there are these proliferations: "by this I am thus", or "by this I am just so", or "by this I am otherwise".
(2) And how is there "by this I am thus"? "By this I am a noble", or "by this I am a brahmin", or "by this I am a merchant", or "by this I am a worker", or "by this I am a householder", or "by this I am a renunciant", or "by this I am a god", or "by this I am a human being", or "by this I have material form", or "by this I am immaterial", or "by this I am percipient", or "by this I am non-percipient", or "by this I am neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by this I am thus".
(3) And how is there "by this I am just so"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, by this so I am a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, by this so I am a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, by this so I am neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by this I am just so".
(4) And how is there "by this I am otherwise"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, by this I am not so a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, by this I am not so a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, by this I am not so neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by this I am otherwise".
(5) And how is there "by this I shall be"? Having taken up some thing — material form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness — one obtains the desire "by this I shall be", one obtains the conceit "by this I shall be", one obtains the view "by this I shall be". When that exists, there are these proliferations: "by this I shall be thus", or "by this I shall be just so", or "by this I shall be otherwise".
(6) And how is there "by this I shall be thus"? "By this I shall be a noble"… or "by this I shall be immaterial", or "by this I shall be percipient", or "by this I shall be non-percipient", or "by this I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by this I shall be thus".
(7) And how is there "by this I shall be just so"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, by this so I shall be a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, by this so I shall be a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, by this so I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by this I shall be just so".
(8) And how is there "by this I shall be otherwise"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, by this I shall not so be a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, by this I shall not so be a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, by this I shall not so be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by this I shall be otherwise".
(9) And how is there "by this I am lasting"? Having taken up some thing — material form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness — one thinks, "by this I am permanent, I am stable, I am eternal, I am not subject to change" — thus there is "by this I am lasting".
(10) And how is there "by this I am perishing"? Having taken up some thing — material form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness — one thinks, "by this I shall be cut off, I shall be destroyed, I shall not be" — thus there is "by this I am perishing".
(11) And how is there "by this may I be"? Having taken up some thing — material form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness — one obtains the desire "by this may I be", one obtains the conceit "by this may I be", one obtains the view "by this may I be". When that exists, there are these proliferations: "by this may I be thus", or "by this may I be just so", or "by this may I be otherwise".
(12) And how is there "by this may I be thus"? "By this may I be a noble", or "by this may I be a brahmin", or "by this may I be a merchant", or "by this may I be a worker", or "by this may I be a householder", or "by this may I be a renunciant", or "by this may I be a god", or "by this may I be a human being", or "by this may I have material form", or "by this may I be immaterial", or "by this may I be percipient", or "by this may I be non-percipient", or "by this may I be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by this may I be thus".
(13) And how is there "by this may I be just so"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, by this so may I be a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, by this so may I be a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, by this so may I be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by this may I be just so".
(14) And how is there "by this may I be otherwise"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, by this may I not so be a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, by this may I not so be a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, by this may I not so be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by this may I be otherwise".
(15) And how is there "by this would that I might be"? Having taken up some thing — material form… feeling… perception… formations… consciousness — one obtains the desire "by this would that I might be", one obtains the conceit "by this would that I might be", one obtains the view "by this would that I might be". When that exists, there are these proliferations: "by this would that I might be thus", or "by this would that I might be just so", or "by this would that I might be otherwise".
(16) And how is there "by this would that I might be thus"? "By this would that I might be a noble", or "by this would that I might be a brahmin", or "by this would that I might be a merchant", or "by this would that I might be a worker", or "by this would that I might be a householder", or "by this would that I might be a renunciant", or "by this would that I might be a god", or "by this would that I might be a human being", or "by this would that I might have material form", or "by this would that I might be immaterial", or "by this would that I might be percipient", or "by this would that I might be non-percipient", or "by this would that I might be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by this would that I might be thus".
(17) And how is there "by this would that I might be just so"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, by this so would that I might be a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, by this so would that I might be a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, by this so would that I might be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by this would that I might be just so".
(18) And how is there "by this would that I might be otherwise"? Comparing oneself with another person: "As he is a noble, by this would that I might not so be a noble", or "as he is a brahmin, by this would that I might not so be a brahmin"… or "as he is neither percipient nor non-percipient, by this would that I might not so be neither percipient nor non-percipient" — thus there is "by this would that I might be otherwise".
These are the eighteen wanderings of craving concerning what is external.
So these are the eighteen wanderings of craving concerning what is internal and these are the eighteen wanderings of craving concerning what is external; gathering them together and summing them up, there are thirty-six wanderings of craving. So there are thirty-six such past wanderings of craving, thirty-six future wanderings of craving, and thirty-six present wanderings of craving; gathering them together and summing them up, there are one hundred and eight wanderings of craving.

Therein, what are the sixty-two grounds of views spoken of by the Blessed One in the exposition of the Brahmajāla? The four eternalist doctrines, the four partly-eternalist doctrines, the four doctrines of the finite and infinite, the four doctrines of endless equivocation, the two doctrines of chance origination, the sixteen doctrines of the percipient, the eight doctrines of the non-percipient, the eight doctrines of the neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, the seven annihilationist doctrines, the five doctrines of Nibbāna in this very life — these are the sixty-two grounds of views spoken of by the Blessed One in the exposition of the Brahmajāla.
The Analysis of the Minor Topics is finished.
Analysis of the Heart of the Teaching
The Section Comprising Everything

How many aggregates are there, how many sense-fields, how many elements, how many truths, how many faculties, how many roots, how many nutriments, how many contacts, how many feelings, how many perceptions, how many intentions, how many minds?
There are five aggregates, twelve sense-fields, eighteen elements, four truths, twenty-two faculties, nine roots, four nutriments, seven contacts, seven feelings, seven perceptions, seven intentions, seven minds.

Therein, what are the five aggregates? The aggregate of material form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, the aggregate of consciousness — these are called "the five aggregates".

Therein, what are the twelve sense-fields? The eye sense-field, the sight sense-field, the ear sense-field, the sound sense-field, the nose sense-field, the smell sense-field, the tongue sense-field, the taste sense-field, the body sense-field, the tangible sense-field, the mind sense-field, the mental-object sense-field — these are called "the twelve sense-fields".

Therein, what are the eighteen elements? The eye element, the sight element, the eye-consciousness element, the ear element, the sound element, the ear-consciousness element, the nose element, the smell element, the nose-consciousness element, the tongue element, the taste element, the tongue-consciousness element, the body element, the tangible element, the body-consciousness element, the mind element, the mental-object element, the mind-consciousness element — these are called "the eighteen elements".
Therein, what are the four truths? The truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, the truth of the path — these are called "the four truths".

Therein, what are the twenty-two faculties? The eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the mind faculty, the faculty of femininity, the faculty of masculinity, the life faculty, the happiness faculty, the pain faculty, the joy faculty, the grief faculty, the equanimity faculty, the faculty of confidence, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, the faculty of "I shall know what is not yet known", the faculty of final knowledge, the faculty of one who has fully known — these are called "the twenty-two faculties".

Therein, what are the nine roots? Three wholesome roots, three unwholesome roots, three neutral roots.
Therein, what are the three wholesome roots? Non-greed is a wholesome root, non-hate is a wholesome root, non-delusion is a wholesome root — these are the three wholesome roots.
Therein, what are the three unwholesome roots? Greed is an unwholesome root, hate is an unwholesome root, delusion is an unwholesome root — these are the three unwholesome roots.
Therein, what are the three neutral roots? Non-greed, non-hate, and non-delusion in the results of wholesome things or in functional neutral things — these are the three neutral roots. These are called "the nine roots".

Therein, what are the four nutriments? The nutriment of solid food, the nutriment of contact, the nutriment of mental intention, the nutriment of consciousness — these are called "the four nutriments".

Therein, what are the seven contacts? Eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, mind-element contact, mind-consciousness-element contact — these are called "the seven contacts".

Therein, what are the seven feelings? Feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, feeling born of nose-contact, feeling born of tongue-contact, feeling born of body-contact, feeling born of mind-element contact, feeling born of mind-consciousness-element contact — these are called "the seven feelings".

Therein, what are the seven perceptions? Perception born of eye-contact, perception born of ear-contact, perception born of nose-contact, perception born of tongue-contact, perception born of body-contact, perception born of mind-element contact, perception born of mind-consciousness-element contact — these are called "the seven perceptions".

Therein, what are the seven intentions? Intention born of eye-contact, intention born of ear-contact, intention born of nose-contact, intention born of tongue-contact, intention born of body-contact, intention born of mind-element contact, intention born of mind-consciousness-element contact — these are called "the seven intentions".

Therein, what are the seven minds? Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, the mind element, the mind-consciousness element — these are called "the seven minds".

At the moment of rebirth in the sense-pleasure element, for all beings five aggregates appear; for some, eleven sense-fields appear; for some, ten sense-fields appear; for some, another ten sense-fields appear; for some, nine sense-fields appear; for some, seven sense-fields appear; for some, eleven elements appear; for some, ten elements appear; for some, another ten elements appear; for some, nine elements appear; for some, seven elements appear; for all, one truth appears; for some, fourteen faculties appear; for some, thirteen faculties appear; for some, another thirteen faculties appear; for some, twelve faculties appear; for some, ten faculties appear; for some, nine faculties appear; for some, another nine faculties appear; for some, eight faculties appear; for some, another eight faculties appear; for some, seven faculties appear; for some, five faculties appear; for some, four faculties appear; for some, three roots appear; for some, two roots appear; some appear without roots; for all, four nutriments appear; for all, one contact appears; for all, one feeling… one perception… one intention… one mind appears.

At the moment of rebirth in the sense-pleasure element, which five aggregates appear for all? The aggregate of material form… the aggregate of consciousness — at the moment of rebirth in the sense-pleasure element, these five aggregates appear for all.

The Section Showing the Different Planes

There are things of the sense sphere and things not of the sense sphere; things of the fine-material sphere and things not of the fine-material sphere; things of the immaterial sphere and things not of the immaterial sphere; things included in a sphere and things not included in any sphere.
Which things are of the sense sphere? Taking as the lower limit the Avīci hell below, and taking as the upper limit the gods who wield power over others' creations, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields that move in this interval and are included here — material form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness — these things are of the sense sphere.
Which things are not of the sense sphere? Things of the fine-material sphere, things of the immaterial sphere, and things not included in any sphere — these things are not of the sense sphere.
Which things are of the fine-material sphere? Taking as the lower limit the Brahmā world below, and taking as the upper limit the Akaniṭṭha gods above, the mind and mental factors of one who has attained, or one who has been reborn there, or one dwelling happily in this very life, that move in this interval and are included here — these things are of the fine-material sphere.
Which things are not of the fine-material sphere? Things of the sense sphere, things of the immaterial sphere, and things not included in any sphere — these things are not of the fine-material sphere.
Which things are of the immaterial sphere? Taking as the lower limit the gods who have reached the field of infinite space below, and taking as the upper limit the gods who have reached the field of neither-perception-nor-non-perception above, the mind and mental factors of one who has attained, or one who has been reborn there, or one dwelling happily in this very life, that move in this interval and are included here — these things are of the immaterial sphere.
Which things are not of the immaterial sphere? Things of the sense sphere, things of the fine-material sphere, and things not included in any sphere — these things are not of the immaterial sphere.
Which things are included? The wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral things subject to mental taints, of the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere: the aggregate of material form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, the aggregate of consciousness — these things are included.
Which things are not included? The paths, the fruits of the paths, and the unconditioned element — these things are not included.
The Section on Generating Action and the Measure of Life
The Generating Action

"Gods": there are three kinds of gods — gods by convention, gods by rebirth, gods by purity.
Gods by convention are kings, queens, and princes.
Gods by rebirth are the gods from the realm of the Four Great Kings upwards.
Gods by purity are the arahants.
Having given gifts, undertaken virtue, and kept the observance day, where are beings reborn? Having given gifts, undertaken virtue, and kept the observance day, some are reborn in the company of wealthy nobles, some are reborn in the company of wealthy brahmins, some are reborn in the company of wealthy householders, some are reborn in the company of the gods of the Four Great Kings, some are reborn in the company of the gods of the Thirty-Three, some are reborn in the company of the Yāma gods, some are reborn in the company of the Tusita gods, some are reborn in the company of the gods who delight in creating, some are reborn in the company of the gods who wield power over others' creations.
The Measure of Life
What is the measure of life of human beings? One hundred years, or a little more.

What is the measure of life of the gods of the Four Great Kings? Fifty human years are one day and night of the gods of the Four Great Kings. Thirty such nights make a month; twelve such months make a year; five hundred such divine years are the measure of life of the gods of the Four Great Kings. How much is that in human reckoning? Nine million years.
What is the measure of life of the gods of the Thirty-Three? One hundred human years are one day and night of the gods of the Thirty-Three. Thirty such nights make a month; twelve such months make a year; one thousand such divine years are the measure of life of the gods of the Thirty-Three. How much is that in human reckoning? Thirty-six million years.
What is the measure of life of the Yāma gods? Two hundred human years are one day and night of the Yāma gods. Thirty such nights make a month; twelve such months make a year; two thousand such divine years are the measure of life of the Yāma gods. How much is that in human reckoning? One hundred and forty-four million years.
What is the measure of life of the Tusita gods? Four hundred human years are one day and night of the Tusita gods. Thirty such nights make a month; twelve such months make a year; four thousand such divine years are the measure of life of the Tusita gods. How much is that in human reckoning? Five hundred and seventy-six million years.
What is the measure of life of the gods who delight in creating? Eight hundred human years are one day and night of the gods who delight in creating. Thirty such nights make a month; twelve such months make a year; eight thousand such divine years are the measure of life of the gods who delight in creating. How much is that in human reckoning? Two thousand three hundred and four million years.
What is the measure of life of the gods who wield power over others' creations? Sixteen hundred human years are one day and night of the gods who wield power over others' creations. Thirty such nights make a month; twelve such months make a year; sixteen thousand such divine years are the measure of life of the gods who wield power over others' creations. How much is that in human reckoning? Nine thousand two hundred and sixteen million years.
These six sense-sphere realms, all abounding in every sense pleasure;
How long is the life of all of them counted as one?
Twelve hundred and twenty-eight crores of years,
And fifty hundred thousand — so it is proclaimed by way of years.

Having developed the first meditative absorption to a limited degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the first meditative absorption to a limited degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods of Brahmā's retinue. What is their measure of life? A third part of an eon.
Having developed the first meditative absorption to a middling degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the first meditative absorption to a middling degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods who are Brahmā's ministers. What is their measure of life? Half an eon.
Having developed the first meditative absorption to a refined degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the first meditative absorption to a refined degree, they are reborn in the company of the Great Brahmā gods. What is their measure of life? An eon.

Having developed the second meditative absorption to a limited degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the second meditative absorption to a limited degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods of limited radiance. What is their measure of life? Two eons.
Having developed the second meditative absorption to a middling degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the second meditative absorption to a middling degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods of measureless radiance. What is their measure of life? Four eons.
Having developed the second meditative absorption to a refined degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the second meditative absorption to a refined degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods of streaming radiance. What is their measure of life? Eight eons.

Having developed the third meditative absorption to a limited degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the third meditative absorption to a limited degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods of limited beauty. What is their measure of life? Sixteen eons.
Having developed the third meditative absorption to a middling degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the third meditative absorption to a middling degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods of measureless beauty. What is their measure of life? Thirty-two eons.
Having developed the third meditative absorption to a refined degree, where are they reborn? Having developed the third meditative absorption to a refined degree, they are reborn in the company of the gods of complete beauty. What is their measure of life? Sixty-four eons.

Having developed the fourth meditative absorption — according to the difference of object, the difference of attention, the difference of desire, the difference of aspiration, the difference of decision, the difference of resolve, the difference of wisdom — some are reborn in the company of the non-percipient gods, some in the company of the Vehapphala gods, some in the company of the Aviha gods, some in the company of the Atappa gods, some in the company of the Sudassa gods, some in the company of the Sudassī gods, some in the company of the Akaniṭṭha gods, some in the company of the gods who have reached the field of infinite space, some in the company of the gods who have reached the field of infinite consciousness, some in the company of the gods who have reached the field of nothingness, some in the company of the gods who have reached the field of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is the measure of life of the non-percipient gods and the Vehapphala gods? Five hundred eons.
What is the measure of life of the Aviha gods? A thousand eons.
What is the measure of life of the Atappa gods? Two thousand eons.
What is the measure of life of the Sudassa gods? Four thousand eons.
What is the measure of life of the Sudassī gods? Eight thousand eons.
What is the measure of life of the Akaniṭṭha gods? Sixteen thousand eons.

What is the measure of life of the gods who have reached the field of infinite space? Twenty thousand eons.
What is the measure of life of the gods who have reached the field of infinite consciousness? Forty thousand eons.
What is the measure of life of the gods who have reached the field of nothingness? Sixty thousand eons.
What is the measure of life of the gods who have reached the field of neither-perception-nor-non-perception? Eighty-four thousand eons.

Lifted up by the power of merit, gone to a destination of sense pleasure or material form,
Having reached even the peak of existence, they come back again to a bad destination.
Beings of such long life still pass away when their life span is exhausted;
No existence whatever is permanent — so said the Great Sage.
Therefore the wise and careful ones, subtle thinkers of what is good,
Develop the highest path for release from aging and death.
Having developed the pure path that plunges into Nibbāna,
Having fully understood all the mental taints, they attain final Nibbāna without taints.
The Section on What Is to Be Directly Known and the Rest

Of the five aggregates, how many are to be directly known, how many are to be fully understood, how many are to be abandoned, how many are to be developed, how many are to be realised, how many are neither to be abandoned, nor to be developed, nor to be realised… of the seven minds, how many are to be directly known, how many are to be fully understood, how many are to be abandoned, how many are to be developed, how many are to be realised, how many are neither to be abandoned, nor to be developed, nor to be realised?

The aggregate of material form is to be directly known and fully understood; it is not to be abandoned, not to be developed, not to be realised. Four aggregates are to be directly known and fully understood; they may be to be abandoned, may be to be developed, may be to be realised, or may be neither to be abandoned, nor to be developed, nor to be realised.
Ten sense-fields are to be directly known and fully understood; they are not to be abandoned, not to be developed, not to be realised. Two sense-fields are to be directly known and fully understood; they may be to be abandoned, may be to be developed, may be to be realised, or may be neither to be abandoned, nor to be developed, nor to be realised.
Sixteen elements are to be directly known and fully understood; they are not to be abandoned, not to be developed, not to be realised. Two elements are to be directly known and fully understood; they may be to be abandoned, may be to be developed, may be to be realised, or may be neither to be abandoned, nor to be developed, nor to be realised.
The truth of the origin is to be directly known, fully understood, and abandoned; it is not to be developed, not to be realised. The truth of the path is to be directly known and fully understood; it is not to be abandoned; it is to be developed; it is not to be realised. The truth of cessation is to be directly known and fully understood; it is not to be abandoned, not to be developed; it is to be realised. The truth of suffering is to be directly known and fully understood; it may be to be abandoned, it is not to be developed, not to be realised, or it may be not to be abandoned.
Nine faculties are to be directly known and fully understood; they are not to be abandoned, not to be developed, not to be realised. The grief faculty is to be directly known, fully understood, and abandoned; it is not to be developed, not to be realised. The faculty of "I shall know what is not yet known" is to be directly known and fully understood; it is not to be abandoned; it is to be developed; it is not to be realised. The faculty of final knowledge is to be directly known and fully understood; it is not to be abandoned; it may be to be developed, or may be to be realised. The faculty of one who has fully known is to be directly known and fully understood; it is not to be abandoned, not to be developed; it is to be realised. Three faculties are to be directly known and fully understood; they are not to be abandoned; they may be to be developed, may be to be realised, or may be not to be developed but to be realised. Six faculties are to be directly known and fully understood; they may be to be abandoned, may be to be developed, may be to be realised, or may be neither to be abandoned, nor to be developed, nor to be realised.

Three wholesome roots are to be directly known and fully understood; they are not to be abandoned; they may be to be developed, are not to be realised, or may be not to be developed. Three neutral roots are to be directly known and fully understood; they are not to be abandoned, not to be developed; they may be to be realised, or may be not to be realised.
The nutriment of solid food is to be directly known and fully understood; it is not to be abandoned, not to be developed, not to be realised. Six contacts are to be directly known and fully understood; they are not to be abandoned, not to be developed, not to be realised. Six feelings… six perceptions… six intentions… six minds are to be directly known and fully understood; they are not to be abandoned, not to be developed, not to be realised. The mind-consciousness element is to be directly known and fully understood; it may be to be abandoned, may be to be developed, may be to be realised, or may be neither to be abandoned, nor to be developed, nor to be realised.
The Section on Having Objects and Not Having Objects
Of the five aggregates, how many have objects, how many are without objects… of the seven minds, how many have objects, how many are without objects?

The aggregate of material form is without an object. Four aggregates have objects.
Ten sense-fields are without objects. The mind sense-field has an object. The mental-object sense-field may have an object, or may be without an object.
Ten elements are without objects. Seven elements have objects. The mental-object element may have an object, or may be without an object.
Two truths have objects. The truth of cessation is without an object. The truth of suffering may have an object, or may be without an object.
Seven faculties are without objects. Fourteen faculties have objects. The life faculty may have an object, or may be without an object. Nine roots have objects. The nutriment of solid food is without an object. Three nutriments have objects. Seven contacts… seven feelings… seven perceptions… seven intentions… seven minds have objects.

Six feelings… six perceptions… six intentions… six minds have things-without-objects as their objects. The Section Showing the Seen, the Heard, and the Rest

Of the five aggregates, how many are seen, how many are heard, how many are sensed, how many are known, how many are neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, but known… of the seven minds, how many are seen, how many are heard, how many are sensed, how many are known, how many are neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, but known?

The aggregate of material form may be seen, may be heard, may be sensed, may be known, or may be neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, but known. Four aggregates are neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, but known.
The sight sense-field is seen, not heard, not sensed, but known. The sound sense-field is not seen, but heard, not sensed, but known. The smell sense-field… the taste sense-field… the tangible sense-field are not seen, not heard, but sensed and known. Seven sense-fields are neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, but known.
The sight element is seen, not heard, not sensed, but known. The sound element is not seen, but heard, not sensed, but known. The smell element… the taste element… the tangible element are not seen, not heard, but sensed and known. Thirteen elements are neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, but known.
Three truths are neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, but known. The truth of suffering may be seen, may be heard, may be sensed, may be known, or may be neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, but known.
The twenty-two faculties are neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, but known. The nine roots are neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, but known. The four nutriments are neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, but known. The seven contacts are neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, but known. The seven feelings… the seven perceptions… the seven intentions… the seven minds are neither seen, nor heard, nor sensed, but known.

The aggregate of material form is material. Four aggregates are immaterial. Ten sense-fields are material. The mind sense-field is immaterial.
